Homer Hickam. American author, engineer, and former NASA employee, best known for his memoir October Sky, published in 1999. This work tells the true story of his high school rocket club in nineteen-fifty-something West Virginia and his path to becoming an aerospace engineer. Hickam represents the democratization of spaceflight aspiration — the engineers who were inspired by Sputnik and the Space Race and built their own rockets from scrap materials.

He founded the Coalwood High School Rocket Club, called the Big Creek Missile Agency or BCMA, in Coalwood, West Virginia, in the late nineteen-fifties. There he and his friends designed and tested solid-fueled rockets from improvised materials. His memoir was adapted into a film starring Jake Gyllenhaal, which became a cultural touchstone for the Space Age and inspired a generation of young engineers.

Hickam worked as an engineer for NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center and later as a payload officer for the Space Shuttle, contributing to the practical continuity of the space program. He represents the grassroots rocket movement of the Space Age — the amateur and student builders who proved that spaceflight was not the exclusive domain of governments and corporate giants.

His story captures the cultural moment when the Soviet Sputnik shocked America and when spaceflight became an accessible dream for working-class teenagers in coal-mining towns. Later, Hickam became a prolific author, writing dozens of books on space history, rockets, and the personal experience of participating in the Space Age.
